references.text: The Lord gives Abraham the original blessing with a promise of land, a great nation, and blessing to all families of the earth—the same 'blessing of Abraham' that Isaac asks for Jacob.

God establishes the covenant with Abraham and promises him the land of Canaan as an eternal possession—'the land where you are living as a foreigner'—a promise that underlies the expression 'the blessing of Abraham.'
God renews Abraham's promise to Isaac: the land, numerous descendants, and blessing to all peoples of the earth—the same blessing that Isaac now passes on to Jacob.
God renews the promise directly to Jacob at Bethel: fruitfulness, nations, kings, and the land given to Abraham and Isaac.
Jacob himself refers to El Shaddai's blessing at Luz (Bethel), where God promised him numerous descendants and the land as an eternal possession—a direct restatement of the blessing from Isaac.
Paul shows that Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, linking the blessing of Abraham to all who believe.
Isaac's blessing to Jacob directly confirms that the covenant terms (land, descendants, foreign status) given to Abraham are now passed on.
Jacob receives confirmation that he inherits the same land promise given to Abraham and Isaac, strengthening his identity as the recipient of the covenant.
The source passage shows the promise given before the journey, while this verse shows the fulfillment of taking possession of the same land promised to the fathers.
Both verses emphasize that ownership of the land rests on God's oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, even though the context varies from blessing to warning.
The source verse is a direct application of the covenant in this passage; both define the status 'foreigner' as a precursor to eternal possession of Canaan.
